description: Great houses, Elizabethan fashion and the rising tide of vagrancy — and the 1601 Poor Law.
content_html:
A Society of Stark Contrasts

Elizabethan England was a society of striking inequality. A small number of landowners — the nobility and gentry — enjoyed wealth, fine houses and elaborate fashions, while at the bottom of society a growing number of the poor struggled to survive. The gap between these extremes widened during the sixteenth century, largely because of rising population, inflation and changes in agriculture. Understanding this contrast is central to understanding the Elizabethan age.

The Lives of the Wealthy

The Elizabethan period saw a wave of great country house building. The great houses built by nobles and wealthy gentry were statements of power and loyalty. Houses such as Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire (built by Bess of Hardwick, completed 1597) and Burghley House in Lincolnshire (built by William Cecil) were designed to impress — and to accommodate the Queen on her summer progresses. Large windows — glass being expensive — were a mark of wealth, leading to the saying “Hardwick Hall, more glass than wall.”

Inside these houses, the wealthy enjoyed lavish feasting. Banquets could last for hours, featuring meat, game, spiced dishes, elaborate sugar sculptures and imported wines. The wealthiest kept their own deer parks for hunting and employed large numbers of servants. A great noble’s household might contain dozens of staff — stewards, cooks, grooms, ladies-in-waiting and more — all reflecting the master’s status.

Dress in Elizabethan England was not merely personal taste — it was a public statement of rank. Sumptuary laws regulated what each social class could wear, reserving certain colours and fabrics for the highest ranks. Purple silk and gold cloth of gold were restricted to royalty. The ruff — the distinctive pleated collar of linen or lace — became a hallmark of the Elizabethan age, growing ever larger and more elaborate across the reign. Wealthy women wore the farthingale, a hooped underskirt that gave skirts their wide, structured shape. These fashions were expensive, time-consuming to maintain and deliberately impractical — they advertised that their wearer did not need to do physical work.

The Lives of the Poor

For the majority of Elizabethans — tenant farmers, labourers, craftsmen and their families — life was far harder. Most people lived in modest timber-framed cottages, working long hours in agriculture or craft trades. Their diet was plain: bread, pottage (a thick vegetable and grain stew), cheese and occasional meat. A poor harvest could mean genuine hunger.

Below the working poor sat an even more desperate group: the vagabonds and vagrants. A rising population — from around 2.8 million in 1551 to approximately 4.1 million by 1601 — combined with inflation (prices rose sharply throughout the reign), enclosures of common land, and the dissolution of the monasteries (which had previously provided some charity) created a growing pool of the homeless and unemployed. Contemporaries feared vagrants as a threat to social order and distinguished between the “impotent poor” (those who could not work due to age, disability or sickness) and the “sturdy beggars” (those deemed capable of work but unwilling to find it).

Key Fact

Four main causes drove the rise of vagrancy: population growth, inflation (rising prices outpacing wages), enclosures of common land (removing livelihoods from rural labourers), and the dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII (removing a traditional source of poor relief).

Government Legislation: The Poor Laws

The Elizabethan government’s response to poverty evolved across the reign. Early measures were harsh: the 1547 Vagrancy Act under Edward VI had briefly enslaved persistent vagrants, though this was quickly repealed. Tudor attitudes were complex — the government felt genuine pity for the “impotent poor” but fear and hostility towards the able-bodied vagrant. A series of poor laws attempted to separate these groups and deal with each differently.

The culmination of Elizabethan poor law legislation came with the 1601 Poor Law (formally the Act for the Relief of the Poor). This act established a national framework by placing responsibility for poor relief on each parish. Overseers of the Poor were appointed in every parish to collect a compulsory “poor rate” from householders and distribute it as follows: the impotent poor (elderly, sick, disabled) received “outdoor relief” — money or goods to allow them to survive at home; the able-bodied poor who genuinely could not find work were to be set to work (in a “house of correction”); and the “idle poor” (sturdy beggars who refused work) were to be punished.

Key Fact

The 1601 Poor Law was landmark legislation: it created a compulsory poor rate in every parish, appointed Overseers of the Poor, and distinguished between the impotent poor (to be helped), the able-bodied unemployed (to be set to work) and idle vagrants (to be punished). It remained the basis of English poor relief for over two hundred years.

The 1601 Poor Law was genuinely significant in the long term. It was the first national, compulsory system of poor relief in English history — a shift from voluntary charity to state obligation. It remained largely in force until the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834. However, its significance in the short term should not be overstated: implementation was uneven, depending on the willingness of local parish officers, and the law did little to address the root causes of poverty such as enclosure and inflation. Critics argue it was more concerned with controlling the poor than genuinely relieving suffering.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Describe two features’ questions about poverty or poor relief, make sure each feature is distinct and specific — for example, “the 1601 Poor Law created a compulsory poor rate” is a precise feature, whereas “the government helped poor people” is too vague for full marks. For 8-mark significance questions, remember to address significance both at the time (immediate impact of the 1601 Poor Law creating a national system) and over time (the act remaining in force until 1834). For 12-mark evaluation questions on whether Elizabeth dealt successfully with poverty, balance evidence of achievement (the 1601 Act) against its limitations (uneven enforcement, no tackling of root causes).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Elizabethan England was sharply divided: wealthy nobles and gentry built great houses, wore elaborate fashions (ruffs, farthingales) and feasted lavishly, while the poor survived on basic food in modest cottages.
  • Vagrancy grew due to four main causes: population growth, inflation, enclosure of common land, and the dissolution of the monasteries removing traditional charity.
  • The 1601 Poor Law was landmark legislation establishing a compulsory parish poor rate and distinguishing between the impotent poor (to be helped), the able-bodied unemployed (to be set to work) and idle vagrants (to be punished). It remained the basis of English poor relief for over two centuries.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the lives of wealthy Elizabethans.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: a precise feature with supporting detail, e.g. wealthy Elizabethans built great houses with large glass windows as a mark of status, such as Hardwick Hall (2 marks). Emerging: a vague feature without specific detail (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1601 Poor Law.
practice_questions.marks: For each feature: Mastering: a precise feature with accurate supporting detail (2 marks). Emerging: a simple feature without development (1 mark). Features may include: it created a compulsory poor rate levied on householders; it appointed Overseers of the Poor in every parish; it distinguished between the impotent poor (to be helped), the able-bodied unemployed (to be set to work) and idle vagrants (to be punished). Maximum 4 marks (2 per feature).

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growth of vagrancy in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a detailed causal chain with evidence, e.g. population growth increased the supply of labour faster than demand, driving wages down and leaving labourers unable to find steady work. Secure: a clear cause with some supporting evidence. Developing: a relevant cause with limited development. Emerging: a simple statement. Maximum 6 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the 1601 Poor Law for Elizabethan England and beyond.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained analysis of significance at the time (first national compulsory system of poor relief; parish-based structure; attempted to categorise and manage the poor) AND over time (remained the basis of English poor law until 1834). Secure: clear explanation with specific evidence. Developing: some explanation with limited range. Emerging: simple descriptive points. Maximum 8 marks.

practice_questions.text: How useful is a contemporary pamphlet describing vagrants as dangerous 'sturdy beggars' for understanding attitudes to poverty in Elizabethan England? Use the source and your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: integrates content (what the pamphlet says about vagrants), provenance (written from an elite/government perspective to justify harsh treatment) and contextual knowledge (the Tudor distinction between the impotent poor and sturdy beggars; the 1601 Act reflecting this attitude) to make a substantiated judgement. Secure: addresses two of the three elements. Developing: mainly describes the source. Emerging: simple comment. Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: 'The government of Elizabeth I dealt effectively with the problem of poverty.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: argues for (the 1601 Poor Law created a national compulsory system; it categorised the poor; it remained in force until 1834) AND against (enforcement was uneven; root causes of inflation and enclosure were not addressed; the law was as much about controlling the poor as relieving them) before reaching a substantiated overall judgement. Secure: both sides with some evidence; clear conclusion. Developing: one-sided response. Emerging: simple agreement. Maximum 12 marks.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following was a key feature of the 1601 Poor Law?
options: It abolished all punishment for vagrants
It gave money to everyone who asked for it
It created a compulsory poor rate in every parish
It built workhouses in every county

knowledge_checks.q: Which fashion item worn by wealthy Elizabethans was a stiff, pleated collar of linen or lace?
The Tudor government distinguished between the 'impotent poor' (who could not work) and the '_____ beggars' (who could work but were deemed unwilling).
One cause of rising vagrancy in Elizabethan England was the _____ of common land, which removed livelihoods from rural labourers.
Match each feature of Elizabethan society to its description:
right: A pleated collar of linen or lace worn as a mark of wealth
A hooped underskirt creating a wide silhouette for wealthy women
Legislation creating a compulsory parish poor rate

flashcard_questions.q: What was the ruff in Elizabethan fashion?
flashcard_questions.a: A stiff, pleated collar of linen or lace, a key symbol of wealth and status.
A hooped underskirt worn by wealthy Elizabethan women to create a wide, structured silhouette.

flashcard_questions.q: Name four causes of the growth of vagrancy in Elizabethan England.
flashcard_questions.a: Population growth, inflation, enclosure of common land, dissolution of the monasteries.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the 'impotent poor' in Elizabethan terminology?
flashcard_questions.a: Those who could not work due to age, disability or sickness — deserving of relief.

flashcard_questions.q: What were 'sturdy beggars' in Elizabethan terminology?
flashcard_questions.a: Able-bodied people deemed capable of work but unwilling to find it — to be punished.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the 1601 Poor Law establish in each parish?
flashcard_questions.a: Overseers of the Poor to collect a compulsory poor rate and distribute relief.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the 1601 Poor Law passed?
flashcard_questions.a: 1601, in the final years of Elizabeth I's reign.

flashcard_questions.q: How long did the 1601 Poor Law framework remain in force?
flashcard_questions.a: Over two hundred years, until the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834.

flashcard_questions.q: What building at Hardwick Hall became famous as a symbol of Elizabethan wealth?
flashcard_questions.a: Its enormous windows — glass was expensive, making them a mark of great wealth.

flashcard_questions.q: The _____ of 1601 created the first national, compulsory system of poor relief in English history.
flashcard_questions.a: Poor Law (Act for the Relief of the Poor).

flashcard_questions.q: What was the main limitation of the 1601 Poor Law?
flashcard_questions.a: Enforcement was uneven and it did not address root causes such as inflation and enclosure.

flashcard_questions.q: What event under Henry VIII removed a traditional source of charity for the poor?

glossary_terms.definition: A large country mansion built by wealthy Elizabethan nobles and gentry, designed to impress and accommodate royal visits.
A stiff, pleated collar of linen or lace worn around the neck, a key symbol of Elizabethan wealth and status.
A hooped underskirt worn by wealthy Elizabethan women to create a wide, structured silhouette in their outer skirts.
Homeless people who wandered the country without a settled home or employment, often associated with idleness and social disorder in Tudor thinking.
Landmark legislation that established a national system of poor relief funded by a compulsory poor rate levied on householders in each parish.
